t: What Is Click-Through Rate (CTR)? How to Calculate and Improve It
d: Click-through rate is the percentage of people who click after seeing your ad, listing, or email. Learn how to calculate CTR and improve it across channels.
s: Click-Through Rate (CTR) The share of people who click after seeing your listing, ad, or email

Click-Through Rate (CTR) The share of people who click after seeing your listing, ad, or email Click-Through Rate (CTR): The percentage of people who click after seeing your ad, search listing, or email link.

What Is Click-Through Rate? Click-through rate, or CTR, measures the percentage of people who click a link after seeing it. The formula is clicks divided by impressions, multiplied by 100. If your ad is shown 1,000 times and earns 50 clicks, your CTR is 5 percent. CTR applies across marketing: search results, Google Ads, social media ads, and emails, where it usually measures clicks divided by emails delivered. Each channel has its own typical ranges, so compare results within the same channel.
Why Click-Through Rate Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses

Why Click-Through Rate Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses CTR shows whether your message stands out. A Mishawaka roofing company may appear in search results thousands of times a month, yet if few people click, that visibility produces little business. Raising CTR turns existing visibility into more visitors and leads. In Google Ads, a strong expected CTR also contributes to Quality Score, which can lower your cost per click. For Northern Indiana businesses on modest budgets, that efficiency adds up. Watching CTR over time also gives early warnings. A sudden drop often signals a new competitor, an outdated offer, or a change on the results page, giving you a chance to respond before leads decline.

How Click-Through Rate Works Impressions The number of times your listing, ad, or email is shown. Clicks The number of times people click through. The calculation CTR equals clicks divided by impressions, times 100. Channel context Search, display, social, and email each have different typical CTRs. Position matters Higher placements in search usually earn higher CTR.

A Local Example A South Bend dental practice sees in Google Search Console that its implants page earns thousands of impressions with a CTR under 1 percent. Its title reads "Services - Smile Dental." It rewrites the title to "Dental Implants in South Bend | Free Consultation " and improves the meta description. Over the next two months, the page's CTR more than doubles at a similar average position. The practice applies the same approach to its other service pages and sees clicks grow without needing higher rankings.

Getting Started With Click-Through Rate Find your CTR data in Google Search Console for organic search, Google Ads for paid search, Meta Ads Manager for social ads, and your email platform for newsletters. Note which pages, ads, or emails have high impressions but low CTR. Improve those first. For search, rewrite title tags and meta descriptions. For ads, test new headlines and offers. For email, write clearer subject lines and stronger calls to action. Change one element at a time, wait for enough data, and compare results.
Quick Wins to Improve Your Click-Through Rate

Quick Wins to Improve Your Click-Through Rate Rewrite titles on high-impression, low-click pages Include the service and town in search titles Test new ad headlines and offers regularly Use clear, benefit-focused email calls to action Add schema to qualify for richer search results

What to Watch For Clicks without conversions. High CTR matters most when visitors also take action. Misleading copy. Clickbait may raise CTR while lowering trust and conversions. AI Overviews. Some searches earn fewer clicks as answers appear on the results page. Small samples. Wait for enough impressions before judging a change.

Click-Through Rate FAQ What is a good CTR? It depends on the channel, industry, and position. Compare your results with your own past performance and similar campaigns. How do I calculate CTR? Divide clicks by impressions and multiply by 100. Does CTR affect SEO? Google has not confirmed CTR as a direct ranking factor, yet higher CTR means more visitors from the rankings you already have. Does CTR affect Google Ads costs? Expected CTR is part of Quality Score, which influences ad rank and cost per click. Why did my CTR drop? Common causes include new competitors, ads or AI Overviews above your listing, ranking changes, or outdated titles. t: What Is Conversion Rate? How to Calculate and Improve It
d: Conversion rate is the percentage of visitors who take a desired action, such as calling or booking. Learn how to calculate it and raise it for your business.
s: Conversion Rate The share of visitors who take the action you want
Conversion Rate The share of visitors who take the action you want Conversion Rate: The percentage of visitors who take the action you want, such as calling, booking, or buying.

What Is Conversion Rate? Conversion rate is the percentage of visitors or recipients who complete a desired action, such as submitting a form, calling, booking an appointment, or making a purchase. The formula is conversions divided by total visitors (or clicks), multiplied by 100. If 1,000 people visit your website in a month and 30 request a quote, your conversion rate is 3 percent. You can measure it for the whole site, for individual pages, or for specific campaigns.
Why Conversion Rate Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses

Why Conversion Rate Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses Conversion rate turns traffic into revenue. A Goshen HVAC company that raises its website conversion rate from 2 to 4 percent doubles its leads without spending another dollar on traffic. It also reveals where marketing is working. Comparing conversion rates by page, channel, and campaign shows which messages and offers resonate with customers across Northern Indiana and Michiana. Even small gains compound. A one-point improvement on a page that receives steady traffic every month adds up to many extra calls and bookings over a year, all from visitors you were already attracting.

How Conversion Rate Works Define the conversion Decide which action counts: calls, forms, bookings, or purchases. Track it Use Google Analytics 4, ad platforms, and call tracking to record each conversion. Calculate Conversions divided by visitors, times 100. Compare segments Look at rates by page, device, channel, and campaign. Test improvements Change headlines, offers, forms, and layouts, then measure.

A Local Example A Plymouth med spa receives steady website traffic, but few visitors book. It shortens its booking form from twelve fields to four, adds before-and-after photos, displays its Google rating near the booking button, and adds a click-to-call button on mobile. Its booking page conversion rate rises noticeably over the following two months. The spa also learns that mobile visitors convert better by calling, so it makes the phone button more prominent on mobile layouts.

Getting Started With Conversion Rate Set up conversion tracking for your most valuable actions, including calls, forms, and bookings. Then find your current conversion rate for the whole site and for your top landing pages in Google Analytics 4. Pick the page with the most traffic and the lowest conversion rate. Review it on a phone, clarify the headline, add trust signals such as reviews and guarantees, shorten the form, and make the call to action obvious. Change one or two things at a time and compare results over several weeks.
Quick Wins to Improve Your Conversion Rate

Quick Wins to Improve Your Conversion Rate Shorten forms to only essential fields Add reviews and trust badges near calls to action Make phone numbers click-to-call on mobile Match landing page headlines to the ad or search Speed up slow pages, especially on phones

What to Watch For Low data. Small numbers swing widely; judge trends over enough visits. Lead quality. A higher rate matters most when leads become customers. Tracking gaps. Untracked calls can make conversion rates look lower than they are. One size fits all. Different pages and channels naturally convert at different rates.

Conversion Rate FAQ What is a good website conversion rate? It varies widely by industry, offer, and traffic source. Compare your pages with your own past results and improve steadily. How do I calculate conversion rate? Divide conversions by visitors or clicks and multiply by 100. What is conversion rate optimization? CRO is the process of testing and improving pages to raise the share of visitors who take action. Should phone calls count as conversions? Yes. For many local businesses, calls are the most valuable conversion. Which pages should I improve first? Start with the pages that receive the most traffic and lead directly to calls or bookings, such as your top service pages and paid ad landing pages. Small gains there produce the biggest results. Does page speed affect conversion rate? Yes. Faster pages generally keep more visitors engaged and lead to more conversions. Put It to Work Want more customers from the traffic you already have? t: What Is Cost Per Click (CPC)? How Ad Pricing Works
d: Cost per click is the amount you pay each time someone clicks your ad. Learn how CPC is set in Google and Meta auctions and how local businesses lower it.
s: Cost Per Click (CPC) The amount you pay each time someone clicks your ad
Cost Per Click (CPC) The amount you pay each time someone clicks your ad Cost Per Click (CPC): The average amount you pay each time someone clicks your ad.

What Is Cost Per Click? Cost per click, or CPC, is the amount an advertiser pays each time someone clicks an ad. Average CPC equals total ad cost divided by total clicks. If you spend $500 and receive 250 clicks, your average CPC is $2. On Google Ads and Microsoft Ads, CPC is set through an auction each time someone searches. Your bid, your ad's quality, and the competition determine your position and price. Social platforms such as Meta often charge by impressions but report CPC as well.
Why Cost Per Click Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses

Why Cost Per Click Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses CPC determines how much traffic your budget can buy. A Valparaiso personal injury law firm may face high CPCs because competition is intense, while a Goshen pet groomer may pay much less. Understanding CPC helps you set realistic budgets and expectations. CPC also connects directly to results. Dividing your cost per lead by your cost per click shows how many clicks it takes to earn a lead, which tells you whether to focus on cheaper traffic or on landing pages that convert more of the clicks you already pay for. Lower CPC means more clicks for the same spend. Improving ad relevance and landing pages can bring CPC down while keeping your ads in strong positions.

How Cost Per Click Works Auction Advertisers compete each time a relevant search happens. Bid The most you are willing to pay for a click. Quality Expected CTR, ad relevance, and landing page experience influence ad rank. Ad rank Bid, quality, and other factors decide your position. Actual CPC You often pay less than your maximum bid, based on the competition.

A Local Example A Goshen dental office pays a high CPC for broad keywords such as "dentist." It shifts budget to more specific searches such as "emergency dentist Goshen" and "dental implants Elkhart County," writes tightly matched ads, and builds dedicated landing pages. Its Quality Scores rise, average CPC falls, and more clicks turn into appointments. The office also adds negative keywords such as "jobs" and "school" so its budget stays focused on patients.
Getting Started With Cost Per Click

Getting Started With Cost Per Click Open your Google Ads Keywords report and sort by cost. Look at average CPC, conversions, and Quality Score for your most expensive keywords to see which ones earn their price. Focus budget on keywords with strong conversion rates, pause or lower bids on expensive keywords that rarely convert, and add negative keywords to block irrelevant searches. Improve ads and landing pages for your core keywords to raise Quality Score, then track how average CPC and cost per lead change.
Quick Wins to Improve Your Cost Per Click

Quick Wins to Improve Your Cost Per Click Focus on specific, high-intent keywords Add negative keywords to block irrelevant searches Improve ad relevance and Quality Score Use location targeting for the towns you serve Schedule ads for the hours customers call

What to Watch For Cheap clicks. Low CPC matters only when clicks turn into customers. Competitive industries. Legal, home services, and finance often have higher CPCs. Broad match. Broad keywords can attract costly, unrelated searches without negatives. Bid wars. Raising bids without improving quality often just raises costs.

Cost Per Click FAQ What is a good CPC? It depends on your industry and the value of a customer. Judge CPC alongside conversion rate and cost per lead. Why are some keywords so expensive? Highly competitive, high-value searches attract many advertisers, which raises prices. How can I lower CPC? Improve Quality Score, use specific keywords, add negatives, and target your service area precisely. Do I pay my maximum bid? Often not. Google charges what is needed to beat the next ad rank, up to your maximum. Is CPC the same on Facebook? Meta often charges by impressions, while reporting CPC so you can compare results. t: What Is Cost Per Lead (CPL)? How to Calculate and Lower It
d: Cost per lead is how much you spend to generate one new lead. Learn how to calculate CPL, what shapes it, and how local businesses lower it.
s: Cost Per Lead (CPL) How much you spend to earn one new lead
Cost Per Lead (CPL) How much you spend to earn one new lead Cost Per Lead (CPL): What each new inquiry costs you, such as a call, form, or booking request.

What Is Cost Per Lead? Cost per lead, or CPL, measures how much marketing spend it takes to generate one new lead, such as a call, form submission, or booking request. The formula is total marketing spend divided by the number of leads. If you spend $1,500 on Google Ads in a month and receive 30 qualified leads, your CPL is $50. You can calculate CPL by channel, campaign, or service to see where leads come most efficiently.
Why Cost Per Lead Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses

Why Cost Per Lead Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses CPL helps small businesses compare channels on equal terms. A Goshen remodeler may find that Google search leads cost more each than Facebook leads, yet close at a much higher rate, which makes search the better investment. Tracking CPL over time also shows whether improvements are working. Better ads, landing pages, and targeting should steadily lower the cost of each lead. CPL also makes budget conversations easier. When you know a lead costs about $50 and roughly one in four becomes a customer, you can plan exactly how much spend it takes to fill next month's schedule.

How Cost Per Lead Works Total spend Include ad spend and, for a full view, management and tool costs. Count leads Track calls, forms, and bookings from each source. Calculate Spend divided by leads. Compare by channel Look at CPL for search, social, email, and other channels. Connect to sales Pair CPL with close rates to see cost per customer.

A Local Example A Michigan City plumbing company spends on Google Ads, Facebook ads, and Local Services Ads. After tracking leads from each, it finds Local Services Ads deliver the lowest CPL for emergency calls, Google Ads deliver the most water heater installation leads, and Facebook ads deliver low-cost leads that rarely book. It shifts Facebook budget toward a remarketing campaign for past customers and increases Local Services Ads during winter, when emergency calls peak. Overall cost per booked job drops.
Getting Started With Cost Per Lead

Getting Started With Cost Per Lead Choose a time period, such as last month, and add up what you spent on each marketing channel. Then count the leads each channel produced using conversion tracking, call tracking, and your CRM. Divide spend by leads to find CPL for each channel. Next, look at how many of those leads became customers, since a slightly higher CPL can still be the better deal if those leads close more often. Review CPL monthly and focus improvements on the channel with the most spend.
Quick Wins to Improve Your Cost Per Lead

Quick Wins to Improve Your Cost Per Lead Track leads separately for each channel Improve landing pages to raise conversion rates Add negative keywords to cut wasted ad clicks Target ads to the towns you actually serve Compare CPL with close rates, not in isolation

What to Watch For Lead quality. The cheapest leads are not always the best customers. Missing calls. Untracked calls make CPL look higher than reality. Seasonality. CPL changes with demand, so compare similar periods. Hidden costs. Include tools and management fees for a complete view.

Cost Per Lead FAQ What is a good cost per lead? It depends on your industry, service value, and close rate. Higher-value services can support a higher CPL. How is CPL different from CAC? CPL measures the cost of a lead. Customer acquisition cost measures the cost of a paying customer. How can I lower my CPL? Improve targeting, ad relevance, landing pages, and conversion rates, and cut spending on low-performing keywords or audiences. Should I include agency fees in CPL? For a complete picture, yes. Many businesses track both ad-only CPL and total CPL. Where do I find CPL data? Ad platforms report cost per conversion for tracked leads. For a full picture, combine ad spend with lead counts from call tracking, form tracking, and your CRM. Does CPL vary by season? Yes. Demand and competition change through the year, so compare similar periods. Put It to Work Want every marketing dollar producing more leads? t: What Is Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)? A Practical Guide
d: Customer acquisition cost is the total cost of winning one new customer. Learn how to calculate CAC and how local businesses use it to guide growth.
s: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) The total cost of winning one new paying customer

Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) The total cost of winning one new paying customer Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC): The total cost to win one new customer, including ads, marketing tools, agency fees, and sales time. CAC is broader than cost per acquisition because it counts every cost, not just ad spend.

What Is Customer Acquisition Cost? Customer acquisition cost, or CAC, is the total amount you spend on marketing and sales to win one new customer. The basic formula is total acquisition costs divided by the number of new customers in the same period. If you spend $6,000 on marketing and sales in a quarter and gain 40 new customers, your CAC is $150. A full calculation can include ad spend, agency or staff costs, software, and sales time.
Why Customer Acquisition Cost Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses

Why Customer Acquisition Cost Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses CAC shows whether growth is profitable. A Warsaw HVAC company that spends $400 to win a customer who brings in thousands of dollars over many years is growing well, while spending more than a customer is worth signals a problem. Knowing CAC also helps you decide how much to invest. When you understand what a new customer costs, you can plan budgets with confidence and compare channels on the cost of real customers rather than clicks or leads.

How Customer Acquisition Cost Works Gather costs Add marketing spend, sales costs, tools, and agency fees for a period. Count new customers Use customers won in the same period. Divide Total costs divided by new customers. Break it down Calculate CAC by channel or campaign when tracking allows. Compare with value Weigh CAC against customer lifetime value.

A Local Example A Goshen IT services company calculates its CAC for the year and finds it spends about $1,200 to win each new managed services client. Each client stays for several years on a monthly contract, so the company decides it can afford to invest more in marketing. Breaking CAC down by channel shows referrals and LinkedIn bring the lowest CAC, so the company adds a structured referral program and expands its LinkedIn content.
Getting Started With Customer Acquisition Cost

Getting Started With Customer Acquisition Cost Choose a period, such as the last quarter or year, and total all marketing and sales costs: ad spend, agency fees, software, and a share of staff time spent on sales and marketing. Count the new customers won in that period, then divide. If your CRM tracks lead sources, calculate CAC by channel as well. Compare CAC with the average value of a customer, and review it every quarter to see whether your marketing is becoming more efficient.
Quick Wins to Improve Your Customer Acquisition Cost

Quick Wins to Improve Your Customer Acquisition Cost Track lead source for every new customer Follow up with leads quickly to raise close rates Build a referral program for happy customers Invest more in channels with the lowest CAC Compare CAC with customer lifetime value

What to Watch For Partial costs. Leaving out sales time or tools makes CAC look lower than it is. Long sales cycles. Customers may close in a later period than the spending that won them. Repeat customers. Count only new customers in CAC. Averages hide detail. CAC by channel reveals where to invest.

Customer Acquisition Cost FAQ What is a good CAC? A healthy CAC is well below the value a customer brings over time. Many businesses aim for lifetime value several times higher than CAC. How is CAC different from cost per lead? Cost per lead measures the cost to generate an inquiry. CAC measures the cost to win a paying customer. How can I lower CAC? Improve close rates, focus on efficient channels, encourage referrals, and nurture leads who are not ready yet. Should CAC include salaries? For a complete picture, include the share of salaries spent on marketing and sales. How often should I calculate CAC? Quarterly is a practical rhythm for most small businesses. t: What Is Customer Lifetime Value (CLV)? How to Calculate It
d: Customer lifetime value is the total revenue or profit a customer brings over the whole relationship. Learn how to calculate CLV and use it to guide marketing.
s: Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) The total value a customer brings over your entire relationship

Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) The total value a customer brings over your entire relationship Customer Lifetime Value (CLV): The total revenue one customer brings your business across the whole relationship. CLV tells you how much a new customer is truly worth.

What Is Customer Lifetime Value? Customer lifetime value, also called CLV, CLTV, or LTV, estimates the total revenue or profit a customer brings to your business over the entire relationship. A simple formula is average purchase value, times purchases per year, times the average number of years a customer stays. If a Mishawaka auto shop customer spends $250 per visit, visits three times a year, and stays for five years, their lifetime value is about $3,750 in revenue. Using profit margin instead of revenue gives a more conservative figure.
Why Customer Lifetime Value Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses

Why Customer Lifetime Value Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses CLV shows how much a customer is truly worth, which changes how much you can afford to spend to win one. A Goshen dentist who knows a family stays for many years can invest confidently in marketing that brings in new families. It also highlights the value of retention. Keeping customers longer and encouraging repeat visits raises CLV, often at a far lower cost than finding new customers. CLV also helps you decide which customers to focus on. When you see that commercial accounts or service plan members stay far longer than one-time buyers, you can shape offers and marketing to attract more customers like them.

How Customer Lifetime Value Works Average purchase value Total revenue divided by number of purchases. Purchase frequency How often a typical customer buys each year. Customer lifespan How many years a typical customer stays. Multiply Value times frequency times lifespan. Adjust for margin Use gross margin for a profit-based CLV.

A Local Example A Goshen pest control company calculates that a typical quarterly-service customer pays about $500 per year and stays for six years, for a lifetime value of about $3,000. Knowing this, the owner is comfortable spending well over the price of a first visit to win each new contract customer. The company also launches a reminder and loyalty program to keep customers longer, raising CLV across its customer base.
Getting Started With Customer Lifetime Value

Getting Started With Customer Lifetime Value Pull a year of sales data and calculate your average purchase value and how often customers buy. Estimate how long a typical customer stays, using your CRM or customer records. Multiply those numbers to estimate CLV, then compare it with customer acquisition cost. Look for ways to raise CLV, such as service plans, reminders, loyalty programs, and helpful follow-up emails, and recalculate once a year.
Quick Wins to Improve Your Customer Lifetime Value

Quick Wins to Improve Your Customer Lifetime Value Offer service plans or memberships Send timely reminders for repeat services Follow up after each purchase with helpful tips Reward referrals and loyalty Compare CLV with CAC to guide marketing spend

What to Watch For Optimistic estimates. Use realistic retention figures based on actual data. Revenue versus profit. Profit-based CLV gives safer spending limits. Segment differences. Different customer groups often have very different CLV. New businesses. Limited history makes early CLV estimates rough.

Customer Lifetime Value FAQ What is a good CLV to CAC ratio? Many businesses aim for lifetime value at least three times acquisition cost, though the right ratio depends on margins and growth plans. How do I raise customer lifetime value? Improve retention, encourage repeat purchases, offer service plans, and build loyalty through great service and helpful communication. Should I use revenue or profit? Profit-based CLV is more conservative and better for setting spending limits. Can email marketing raise CLV? Yes. Reminders, tips, and offers keep customers coming back. Does CLV matter for one-time services? Yes. Even one-time customers bring referrals and reviews, and many businesses discover related services those customers would happily buy again. How often should I calculate CLV? Once or twice a year is enough for most small businesses. Put It to Work Want to know what your customers are truly worth and how to keep them longer? AI Referral Traffic Share Website & SEO The share of your website visits that arrive from AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Copilot. Formula AI referral share = Visits from AI assistants ÷ Total website visits × 100 Example: A Fort Wayne accounting firm gets 4,000 visits in a month and 80 come from AI assistants. 80 ÷ 4,000 × 100 = 2%. Why it matters: This channel is growing, so tracking it now gives you a baseline to measure against. See also: Share of Voice, Organic Traffic Growth Rate Ask Riley about AI Referral Traffic Share → Explore AI Optimization →

Average Engagement Time Website & SEO The average time your website was actively in focus on a visitor’s screen, as reported by Google Analytics 4. Formula Average engagement time = Total engagement time ÷ Number of active users Example: A Warsaw orthopedic clinic’s knee pain guide totals 50 hours (3,000 minutes) of engagement from 1,500 users. 3,000 ÷ 1,500 = 2 minutes average engagement time. Why it matters: Longer engagement on key pages often signals content that answers real questions. See also: Engagement Rate (Website), Bounce Rate Ask Riley about Average Engagement Time → Explore Search Engine Optimization →

Average Order Value (AOV) Sales & Customers The average amount a customer spends per order or job. Formula AOV = Total revenue ÷ Number of orders Example: A South Bend boutique earns $18,000 from 300 orders in a month. $18,000 ÷ 300 = $60 average order value. Why it matters: Bundles, add-ons, and free shipping thresholds raise AOV without new customers. See also: Customer Lifetime Value (CLV), Repeat Purchase Rate Ask Riley about Average Order Value →

Average Position Website & SEO Where your pages typically appear in Google search results for a keyword or group of keywords, as reported in Google Search Console. Position 1 is the top. Formula Average position = Sum of top positions across impressions ÷ Number of impressions Example: A Granger pizza shop’s page shows at position 2 for 300 impressions and position 4 for 100 impressions. ((2 × 300) + (4 × 100)) ÷ 400 = 2.5 average position. Why it matters: Track positions for the searches that bring calls, not just the ones with the most volume. See also: Search Click-Through Rate, Organic Traffic Growth Rate, Local Pack Visibility Ask Riley about Average Position → Explore Search Engine Optimization →

Bounce Rate Website & SEO In Google Analytics 4, the percentage of sessions that were not engaged. It is the opposite of engagement rate. Formula Bounce rate = 100% − Engagement rate Example: A South Bend restaurant’s menu page has a 62% engagement rate, so its bounce rate is 100% − 62% = 38%. After compressing photos, engagement rises and bounce rate falls. Why it matters: Check bounce rate by page. A contact page and a blog post naturally behave differently. See also: Engagement Rate (Website), Average Engagement Time Ask Riley about Bounce Rate → Explore Website Design →

Break-Even ROAS Advertising The return on ad spend where your ads exactly cover their own cost. Any ROAS above this number adds profit. Formula Break-even ROAS = 1 ÷ Profit margin (as a decimal) Example: A Middlebury furniture showroom earns a 25% profit margin. 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4, so every $1 of ad spend needs $4 in sales to break even. Why it matters: Set this number before a campaign starts so everyone knows what success looks like. See also: Return on Ad Spend (ROAS), Return on Investment (ROI) Ask Riley about Break-Even ROAS → Explore Paid Search Ads →

CAC Payback Period Sales & Customers How many months it takes for a new customer to earn back what you spent to win them. Formula CAC payback period = CAC ÷ Monthly gross profit per customer Example: An Elkhart gym spends $120 to win a member who brings in $40 of gross profit each month. $120 ÷ $40 = a 3-month payback period. Why it matters: Shorter payback periods free up cash sooner to reinvest in growth. See also: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC), Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) Ask Riley about CAC Payback Period →

Churn Rate Sales & Customers The percentage of customers who stop buying or cancel during a period. Churn is the flip side of retention. Formula Churn rate = Customers lost during the period ÷ Customers at start × 100 Example: A Granger fitness studio starts the month with 250 members and 10 cancel. 10 ÷ 250 × 100 = 4% monthly churn. Why it matters: Watch which customers leave and when. Patterns point to the fix. See also: Customer Retention Rate, Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) Ask Riley about Churn Rate →

Click Rate Email & SMS The percentage of delivered emails or texts where at least one link was clicked. Formula Click rate = Unique clicks ÷ Messages delivered × 100 Example: A Nappanee furniture store delivers 1,200 emails and 48 people click. 48 ÷ 1,200 × 100 = 4% click rate. Why it matters: One clear call to action per message usually earns the most clicks. See also: Click-to-Open Rate (CTOR), Open Rate, Revenue per Email Ask Riley about Click Rate → Explore Email Marketing →

Click-Through Rate (CTR) Advertising The percentage of people who click after seeing your ad, search listing, or email link. Formula CTR = Clicks ÷ Impressions × 100 Example: A Niles dentist’s ad appears 1,000 times and earns 50 clicks. 50 ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 5% CTR. Why it matters: A strong CTR means your headline and offer match what people are looking for. See also: Impressions, Cost Per Click (CPC), Conversion Rate Read the full guide → Explore Paid Search Ads →

Click-to-Open Rate (CTOR) Email & SMS The percentage of people who opened an email and then clicked a link. It measures how well the content inside the email performs. Formula CTOR = Unique clicks ÷ Unique opens × 100 Example: A Goshen garden center’s email gets 300 opens and 45 clicks. 45 ÷ 300 × 100 = 15% CTOR. Why it matters: Use CTOR to compare email designs and offers fairly. See also: Click Rate, Open Rate Ask Riley about Click-to-Open Rate → Explore Email Marketing →

CLV to CAC Ratio Sales & Customers Compares what a customer is worth with what it cost to win them. It shows whether your growth is healthy and where you have room to invest more. Formula CLV:CAC ratio = Customer lifetime value ÷ Customer acquisition cost Example: A Mishawaka dental practice has a patient lifetime value of $3,600 and a CAC of $300. $3,600 ÷ $300 = 12, a 12:1 ratio, so the practice can confidently invest more in attracting patients. Why it matters: A ratio around 3:1 is a common rule of thumb. Higher ratios mean you can grow faster with confidence. See also: Customer Lifetime Value (CLV), Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) Ask Riley about CLV to CAC Ratio →

Conversion Rate Website & SEO The percentage of visitors who take the action you want, such as calling, booking, or buying. Formula Conversion rate = Conversions ÷ Visitors (or sessions) × 100 Example: A Middlebury furniture showroom receives 400 website visitors in a month and 20 of them book a visit. 20 ÷ 400 × 100 = 5% conversion rate. Why it matters: Small improvements here multiply the value of every visitor you already have. See also: Landing Page Conversion Rate, Click-Through Rate (CTR), Bounce Rate Read the full guide → Explore Website Design →

Cost Per Acquisition (CPA) Advertising The ad spend needed to win one conversion, such as a sale, booking, or signed customer. CPA focuses on ad spend for a campaign, while CAC includes every cost. Formula CPA = Ad spend ÷ Number of conversions Example: A Mishawaka remodeler spends $500 on ads and signs 10 new customers. $500 ÷ 10 = $50 CPA. Why it matters: Set a target CPA based on what a customer is worth, and let it guide bids and budgets. See also: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC), Cost Per Lead (CPL), Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) Ask Riley about Cost Per Acquisition → Explore Paid Search Ads →

Cost Per Click (CPC) Advertising The average amount you pay each time someone clicks your ad. Formula CPC = Ad spend ÷ Clicks Example: A Goshen plumber spends $650 on search ads and receives 100 clicks. $650 ÷ 100 = $6.50 CPC. Why it matters: Higher quality ads and landing pages often earn lower click costs on Google. See also: Click-Through Rate (CTR), Cost Per Lead (CPL), Cost Per Thousand Impressions (CPM) Read the full guide → Explore Paid Search Ads →

Cost Per Lead (CPL) Advertising What each new inquiry costs you, such as a call, form, or booking request. Formula CPL = Marketing spend ÷ Number of leads Example: A Warsaw home builder spends $600 on ads in one month and receives 20 inquiries. $600 ÷ 20 = $30 CPL. Why it matters: Compare CPL with your close rate to see what each new customer really costs. See also: Lead-to-Customer Rate (Close Rate), Cost Per Acquisition (CPA), Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) Read the full guide → Explore Paid Search Ads →

Cost Per Thousand Impressions (CPM) Advertising The price you pay for every 1,000 times your ad appears. CPM is common for awareness campaigns on social media, display, and streaming. Formula CPM = Ad spend ÷ Impressions × 1,000 Example: A Goshen boutique spends $200 and its ad appears 40,000 times. $200 ÷ 40,000 × 1,000 = $5 CPM. Why it matters: Use CPM to compare how affordably different platforms reach your audience. See also: Impressions, Reach, Cost Per Click (CPC) Ask Riley about Cost Per Thousand Impressions → Explore Paid Social Media Ads →

Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) Sales & Customers The total cost to win one new customer, including ads, marketing tools, agency fees, and sales time. CAC is broader than cost per acquisition because it counts every cost, not just ad spend. Formula CAC = Total sales and marketing costs ÷ Number of new customers Example: A Warsaw landscaping company spends $4,500 in a quarter on ads, software, and marketing help, and signs 30 new customers. $4,500 ÷ 30 = $150 CAC. Why it matters: Pair CAC with customer lifetime value to see how much you can afford to spend to grow. See also: Cost Per Acquisition (CPA), Customer Lifetime Value (CLV), CLV to CAC Ratio, CAC Payback Period Read the full guide → Explore HubSpot Setup →

Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) Sales & Customers The total revenue one customer brings your business across the whole relationship. CLV tells you how much a new customer is truly worth. Formula CLV = Average purchase value × Purchases per year × Average years as a customer Example: A Middlebury lawn care customer pays $150 per visit, books 12 visits a year, and stays 5 years. $150 × 12 × 5 = $9,000 lifetime value. Why it matters: Multiply CLV by your profit margin to see lifetime profit, the number to compare with CAC. See also: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC), CLV to CAC Ratio, Customer Retention Rate, Average Order Value (AOV) Read the full guide →

Customer Retention Rate Sales & Customers The percentage of existing customers who stay with you over a period. Keeping customers usually costs less than finding new ones. Formula Retention rate = (Customers at end − New customers gained) ÷ Customers at start × 100 Example: A Goshen auto shop starts the year with 400 customers, gains 120 new ones, and ends with 460. (460 − 120) ÷ 400 × 100 = 85% retention. Why it matters: Email, SMS reminders, and great service all raise retention. See also: Churn Rate, Customer Lifetime Value (CLV), Repeat Purchase Rate Ask Riley about Customer Retention Rate → Explore Email Marketing →

Delivery Rate Email & SMS The percentage of emails or texts that reached the recipient’s inbox or phone without bouncing or failing. Formula Delivery rate = Messages delivered ÷ Messages sent × 100 Example: A Granger med spa sends 2,000 emails and 1,960 are delivered. 1,960 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 98% delivery rate. Why it matters: Clean lists and proper email authentication keep delivery rates high. See also: Email Bounce Rate, Open Rate, Spam Complaint Rate Ask Riley about Delivery Rate → Explore Email Marketing →

Email Bounce Rate Email & SMS The percentage of sent emails that could not be delivered. Hard bounces come from invalid addresses and soft bounces from temporary problems such as full inboxes. Formula Email bounce rate = Bounced emails ÷ Emails sent × 100 Example: A South Bend nonprofit sends 3,000 emails and 45 bounce. 45 ÷ 3,000 × 100 = 1.5% bounce rate. Why it matters: Remove hard bounces right away to protect your sender reputation. See also: Delivery Rate, Spam Complaint Rate Ask Riley about Email Bounce Rate → Explore Email Marketing →

Engagement Rate (Social) Social Media The percentage of people who interacted with your post through likes, comments, shares, or saves, compared with how many people saw it. Formula Engagement rate = Total engagements ÷ Reach × 100 Example: A Michigan City boutique’s reel reaches 2,400 people and earns 120 interactions. 120 ÷ 2,400 × 100 = 5% engagement rate. Why it matters: Some platforms divide by impressions or followers instead, so compare numbers using the same method. See also: Reach, Follower Growth Rate, Engagement Rate (Website) Ask Riley about Engagement Rate → Explore Social Media Marketing →

Engagement Rate (Website) Website & SEO In Google Analytics 4, the percentage of sessions that were engaged. GA4 counts a session as engaged when it lasts longer than 10 seconds, includes a key event, or has at least two page views. Formula Engagement rate = Engaged sessions ÷ Total sessions × 100 Example: A Goshen law firm’s site has 1,000 sessions and 620 are engaged. 620 ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 62% engagement rate. Why it matters: Clear headlines, fast pages, and helpful next steps raise engagement. See also: Bounce Rate, Average Engagement Time, Conversion Rate Ask Riley about Engagement Rate → Explore Website Design →

Follower Growth Rate Social Media How quickly your social following is growing over a period. Formula Follower growth rate = New followers gained ÷ Followers at start × 100 Example: An Elkhart bakery starts the month with 2,000 Instagram followers and gains 150. 150 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 7.5% growth. Why it matters: Steady growth from local followers matters more than a big one-time spike. See also: Engagement Rate (Social), Reach Ask Riley about Follower Growth Rate → Explore Social Media Marketing →

Frequency Advertising The average number of times one person sees your ad. Formula Frequency = Impressions ÷ Reach Example: An ad shown 6,000 times to 2,000 people in Elkhart County has a frequency of 6,000 ÷ 2,000 = 3. Why it matters: Moderate frequency builds familiarity. When results dip as frequency climbs, refresh the creative. See also: Reach, Impressions Ask Riley about Frequency → Explore Paid Social Media Ads →

Impressions Advertising The number of times your ad, post, or listing appears on a screen. One person can create several impressions. Formula Impressions = Total times content was displayed Example: A Mishawaka dentist’s search ad appears 10,000 times in one month. That total is 10,000 impressions. Why it matters: Impressions measure visibility. Pair them with clicks and conversions to see results. See also: Reach, Click-Through Rate (CTR), Cost Per Thousand Impressions (CPM), Impression Share Ask Riley about Impressions → Explore Paid Search Ads →

Impression Share Advertising The percentage of available impressions your ads actually received. It shows how much more of the market you could reach. Formula Impression share = Impressions received ÷ Estimated impressions available × 100 Example: A Middlebury furniture showroom’s ad appeared 4,000 times out of about 10,000 possible. 4,000 ÷ 10,000 × 100 = 40% impression share. Why it matters: Budget and ad rank both affect impression share, and Google Ads reports which one is holding you back. See also: Impressions, Click-Through Rate (CTR) Ask Riley about Impression Share → Explore Paid Search Ads →

Landing Page Conversion Rate Advertising The percentage of visitors to a specific landing page who complete its goal, such as a form or call. Formula Landing page conversion rate = Conversions on the page ÷ Visitors to the page × 100 Example: A LaGrange County dentist’s whitening offer page gets 500 visits from ads and 40 bookings. 40 ÷ 500 × 100 = 8%. Why it matters: One clear offer and one clear button usually convert best. See also: Conversion Rate, Cost Per Lead (CPL) Ask Riley about Landing Page Conversion Rate → Explore Website Design →

Lead-to-Customer Rate (Close Rate) Sales & Customers The percentage of leads that become paying customers. It shows how well your follow-up and sales process turn interest into revenue. Formula Close rate = New customers ÷ Total leads × 100 Example: A Plymouth roofing company receives 60 estimate requests in a month and signs 15 jobs. 15 ÷ 60 × 100 = 25% close rate. Why it matters: Fast follow-up and clear quotes are two of the quickest ways to raise close rate. See also: Cost Per Lead (CPL), Win Rate, MQL to SQL Conversion Rate Ask Riley about Lead-to-Customer Rate → Explore HubSpot Setup →

List Growth Rate Email & SMS How fast your email or SMS subscriber list is growing after accounting for people who leave. Formula List growth rate = (New subscribers − Unsubscribes and removals) ÷ Starting list size × 100 Example: A South Bend coffee shop starts the month with 1,000 subscribers, gains 80, and loses 20. (80 − 20) ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 6% growth. Why it matters: In-store sign-up offers and website forms are steady growth sources for local businesses. See also: Unsubscribe Rate, Delivery Rate Ask Riley about List Growth Rate → Explore SMS Marketing →

Local Pack Visibility Website & SEO How often your business appears in the Google map results, often called the Local Pack, across the searches and neighborhoods you care about. Grid-based rank trackers measure it by checking results from many points on a map. Formula Local Pack visibility = Grid points where you rank in the top 3 ÷ Total grid points checked × 100 Example: A Goshen HVAC company checks a 25-point grid around town and appears in the top 3 at 15 points. 15 ÷ 25 × 100 = 60% visibility. Why it matters: Reviews, profile completeness, and nearby relevance all move this number. See also: Average Position, Review Rating Average, Review Velocity Ask Riley about Local Pack Visibility → Explore Local SEO →

MQL to SQL Conversion Rate Sales & Customers The share of marketing qualified leads (people who showed interest) that sales accepts as sales qualified leads (people ready for a sales conversation). Formula MQL to SQL rate = Sales qualified leads ÷ Marketing qualified leads × 100 Example: An Elkhart manufacturer gets 80 marketing qualified leads from a trade guide download, and sales qualifies 20 of them. 20 ÷ 80 × 100 = 25%. Why it matters: A rising rate means marketing and sales agree on what a good lead looks like. See also: Lead-to-Customer Rate (Close Rate), Win Rate Ask Riley about MQL to SQL Conversion Rate → Explore HubSpot Setup →

Open Rate Email & SMS The percentage of delivered emails that were opened. Privacy features such as Apple Mail Privacy Protection can count opens automatically, so treat open rate as a directional signal. Formula Open rate = Unique opens ÷ Emails delivered × 100 Example: A Granger fitness studio delivers a newsletter to 500 subscribers and 140 open it. 140 ÷ 500 × 100 = 28% open rate. Why it matters: Clicks and conversions tell a more reliable story than opens alone. See also: Click Rate, Click-to-Open Rate (CTOR), Delivery Rate Ask Riley about Open Rate → Explore Email Marketing →

Organic Traffic Growth Rate Website & SEO How much your unpaid search traffic grew from one period to the next. Formula Growth rate = (This period’s organic visits − Last period’s) ÷ Last period’s × 100 Example: An Elkhart roofer’s organic visits rise from 800 in March to 1,000 in April. (1,000 − 800) ÷ 800 × 100 = 25% growth. Why it matters: Compare the same months year over year to account for seasonal swings. See also: Average Position, Search Click-Through Rate Ask Riley about Organic Traffic Growth Rate → Explore Search Engine Optimization →

Pipeline Value (Weighted) Sales & Customers The expected value of open deals, adjusted by how likely each one is to close. It turns your sales pipeline into a realistic forecast. Formula Weighted pipeline = Sum of (Deal value × Close probability) Example: A Goshen sign company has a $10,000 deal at 50% and a $6,000 deal at 25%. ($10,000 × 0.5) + ($6,000 × 0.25) = $6,500 weighted pipeline. Why it matters: Update probabilities as deals move stages so the forecast stays honest. See also: Win Rate, Sales Cycle Length Ask Riley about Pipeline Value → Explore HubSpot Setup →

Reach Advertising The number of unique people who saw your content. Reach counts each person once, while impressions count every view. Formula Reach = Unique people who saw your content Example: A Michigan City boutique’s post appears on 3,000 screens but belongs to 2,000 different people. Reach is 2,000 and impressions are 3,000. Why it matters: Growing reach means new people are discovering your business. See also: Impressions, Frequency, Engagement Rate (Social) Ask Riley about Reach → Explore Paid Social Media Ads →

Repeat Purchase Rate Sales & Customers The percentage of customers who buy from you more than once. It measures loyalty and how well your follow-up works. Formula Repeat purchase rate = Customers with 2 or more purchases ÷ Total customers × 100 Example: A Nappanee bakery has 800 customers this year, and 320 of them ordered more than once. 320 ÷ 800 × 100 = 40% repeat purchase rate. Why it matters: Loyalty offers, reminders, and email series lift this number. See also: Customer Retention Rate, Average Order Value (AOV) Ask Riley about Repeat Purchase Rate → Explore Email Marketing →

Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) Advertising The revenue you earn for every dollar you spend on ads. ROAS shows how hard your ad budget is working. Formula ROAS = Revenue from ads ÷ Ad spend Example: An Elkhart RV supplier spends $2,000 on ads and generates $8,000 in sales. $8,000 ÷ $2,000 = a ROAS of 4, or $4 back for every $1 spent. Why it matters: Compare ROAS with your break-even ROAS to see whether ads are adding profit. See also: Break-Even ROAS, Return on Investment (ROI), Cost Per Acquisition (CPA) Read the full guide → Explore Paid Search Ads →

Return on Investment (ROI) Business Results How much profit an investment returns compared with what it cost. ROI is the clearest way to judge whether marketing is paying for itself. Formula ROI = (Gain from investment − Cost of investment) ÷ Cost of investment × 100 Example: A Niles remodeler spends $1,000 on marketing and earns $4,000 in new business from it. ($4,000 − $1,000) ÷ $1,000 × 100 = 300% ROI. Why it matters: Use profit, not revenue, as the gain when you can. It shows what you actually keep. See also: Return on Marketing Investment (ROMI), Return on Ad Spend (ROAS), Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) Read the full guide →

Return on Marketing Investment (ROMI) Business Results ROI measured for marketing alone. It compares the gross profit your marketing brings in with what the marketing cost, including fees and tools. Formula ROMI = (Gross profit from marketing − Marketing cost) ÷ Marketing cost × 100 Example: A Goshen HVAC company spends $3,000 in a month on ads, software, and agency fees. Those campaigns bring in $9,000 of gross profit. ($9,000 − $3,000) ÷ $3,000 × 100 = 200% ROMI. Why it matters: Counting every marketing cost gives you an honest number to compare channels and months. See also: Return on Investment (ROI), Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) Ask Riley about Return on Marketing Investment →

Revenue per Email Email & SMS The average revenue each delivered email produced. It turns email results into dollars. Formula Revenue per email = Revenue from the campaign ÷ Emails delivered Example: A Goshen boutique’s holiday email earns $2,400 from 4,000 delivered emails. $2,400 ÷ 4,000 = $0.60 per email. Why it matters: Compare this across campaigns to find your most valuable message types. See also: Click Rate, Return on Investment (ROI) Ask Riley about Revenue per Email → Explore Email Marketing →

Review Rating Average Website & SEO Your average star rating across reviews on a platform such as Google. Formula Average rating = Sum of all star ratings ÷ Number of reviews Example: A Middlebury cafe has 40 reviews totaling 188 stars. 188 ÷ 40 = 4.7 average rating. Why it matters: Respond to every review. Thoughtful replies build trust with future customers. See also: Review Velocity, Local Pack Visibility Ask Riley about Review Rating Average → Explore Local SEO →

Review Velocity Website & SEO How many new reviews your business earns in a set period. A steady flow shows customers and search engines that you are active and trusted. Formula Review velocity = New reviews ÷ Number of months Example: A Mishawaka auto shop earns 36 new Google reviews in 6 months. 36 ÷ 6 = 6 reviews per month. Why it matters: Asking right after a great experience is the simplest way to keep reviews coming. See also: Review Rating Average, Local Pack Visibility Read the full guide → Explore Local SEO →

Sales Cycle Length Sales & Customers The average number of days between first contact and a closed sale. Formula Sales cycle length = Total days to close for all won deals ÷ Number of won deals Example: A Mishawaka commercial cleaner closes 5 contracts that took 20, 25, 30, 35, and 40 days. 150 ÷ 5 = a 30-day average sales cycle. Why it matters: Knowing your cycle helps you plan cash flow and time campaigns ahead of busy seasons. See also: Win Rate, Pipeline Value (Weighted) Ask Riley about Sales Cycle Length → Explore HubSpot Setup →

Search Click-Through Rate Website & SEO The percentage of people who click your page after seeing it in unpaid search results, as reported by Google Search Console. Formula Search CTR = Clicks from search ÷ Search impressions × 100 Example: A Mishawaka dentist’s cleaning page earns 120 clicks from 3,000 search impressions. 120 ÷ 3,000 × 100 = 4%. Why it matters: Sharper title tags and meta descriptions often lift search CTR. See also: Average Position, Click-Through Rate (CTR) Ask Riley about Search Click-Through Rate → Explore Search Engine Optimization →

Share of Voice Website & SEO Your share of the attention in your market compared with competitors. It can be measured in search visibility, ad impressions, social mentions, or AI answers. Formula Share of voice = Your mentions or visibility ÷ Total for you and competitors × 100 Example: When 20 AI answers about “best Elkhart plumber” are checked, a plumbing company appears in 6. 6 ÷ 20 × 100 = 30% AI share of voice. Why it matters: Pick one measurement method and track it consistently over time. See also: Impression Share, Local Pack Visibility Ask Riley about Share of Voice → Explore AI Optimization →

Social Referral Traffic Social Media Website visits that come from social media platforms. It shows whether your posts move people from scrolling to your site. Formula Social referral share = Visits from social ÷ Total website visits × 100 Example: A Goshen boutique’s website gets 2,000 visits in a month and 300 come from Facebook and Instagram. 300 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 15% from social. Why it matters: Add UTM parameters to social links for the clearest reporting. See also: Engagement Rate (Social), Conversion Rate Ask Riley about Social Referral Traffic → Explore Social Media Marketing →

Spam Complaint Rate Email & SMS The percentage of recipients who mark your email as spam. Gmail’s sender guidelines ask bulk senders to keep this below 0.3%, and lower is better. Formula Spam complaint rate = Spam complaints ÷ Emails delivered × 100 Example: A Mishawaka retailer delivers 10,000 emails and receives 5 complaints. 5 ÷ 10,000 × 100 = 0.05%. Why it matters: Clear opt-ins and an easy unsubscribe link protect your inbox placement. See also: Unsubscribe Rate, Delivery Rate Ask Riley about Spam Complaint Rate → Explore Email Marketing →

t: What Is Return on Ad Spend (ROAS)? How to Calculate It
d: Return on ad spend measures the revenue earned for every dollar spent on ads. Learn how to calculate ROAS, set targets, and improve it.
s: Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) The revenue you earn for every dollar you spend on ads

Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) The revenue you earn for every dollar you spend on ads Return on Ad Spend (ROAS): The revenue you earn for every dollar you spend on ads. ROAS shows how hard your ad budget is working.
What Is Return on Ad Spend?

What Is Return on Ad Spend? Return on ad spend, or ROAS, measures how much revenue your advertising generates for each dollar spent. The formula is revenue from ads divided by ad spend. If $1,000 in ads produces $5,000 in sales, your ROAS is 5, often written as 5:1 or 500 percent. ROAS focuses only on advertising costs and the revenue those ads produce. It is narrower than return on investment, which accounts for all costs, including products, labor, and overhead.
Why Return on Ad Spend Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses

Why Return on Ad Spend Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses ROAS shows which ads truly pay off. A Goshen furniture store may find that Google Shopping ads return 8 dollars for every dollar while a broad display campaign returns 1.5, which makes the next budget decision clear. For service businesses across Northern Indiana, ROAS connects ad spending to booked jobs and contracts, as long as leads are tracked through to revenue in a CRM or sales records. ROAS also keeps budgets honest during busy seasons. When demand rises and ad costs climb, comparing ROAS week over week shows whether higher spending is still producing profitable sales or simply buying more expensive clicks.
How Return on Ad Spend Works

How Return on Ad Spend Works Track revenue Connect ad conversions to actual sales values. Track spend Record total ad spend for the same period and campaign. Calculate Revenue divided by ad spend. Compare campaigns Find which campaigns and channels earn the highest return. Set a target Use your margins to determine the minimum profitable ROAS.

A Local Example A Valparaiso landscaping company spends $3,000 on Google Ads over a spring season. By tracking which leads become signed projects in its CRM, it attributes $24,000 in revenue to the ads, for a ROAS of 8. Patio and hardscape campaigns show the highest return, while general lawn care campaigns return less. The company shifts budget toward hardscape campaigns the following spring and keeps a smaller lawn care campaign focused on its best towns.
Getting Started With Return on Ad Spend

Getting Started With Return on Ad Spend Make sure you can connect ad leads to revenue. For online sales, ecommerce tracking handles this. For service businesses, record the lead source in your CRM and note the value of each closed job. Calculate ROAS for each campaign over a meaningful period, such as a quarter. Then figure out your break-even ROAS using your profit margin: if your margin is 40 percent, you need a ROAS of at least 2.5 to cover ad costs. Shift budget toward campaigns comfortably above that line.
Quick Wins to Improve Your Return on Ad Spend

Quick Wins to Improve Your Return on Ad Spend Connect ad leads to closed revenue in your CRM Calculate break-even ROAS using your profit margin Compare ROAS by campaign and channel Shift budget toward the highest-return campaigns Use Target ROAS bidding once you have enough data

What to Watch For Revenue versus profit. A high ROAS on low-margin products may still lose money. Long sales cycles. Revenue may arrive months after the ad spend. Attribution. Customers often see several touchpoints before buying. Missing offline sales. Phone and in-person sales need tracking too.

Return on Ad Spend FAQ What is a good ROAS? It depends on your margins. A business with high margins can profit at a lower ROAS than one with thin margins. How is ROAS different from ROI? ROAS measures revenue against ad spend. ROI measures profit against total investment. How do I calculate break-even ROAS? Divide 1 by your profit margin. A 25 percent margin requires a ROAS of 4 to break even. Can service businesses use ROAS? Yes, by tracking which ad leads become paying customers and their value. What is Target ROAS? A Google Ads bid strategy that aims for a specific return on ad spend. Put It to Work Want to know exactly what your ads earn? t: What Is Marketing ROI? How to Measure Return on Investment
d: Return on investment compares the profit from marketing with what it cost. Learn how to calculate marketing ROI and use it to make confident decisions.
s: Return on Investment (ROI) The profit your marketing returns compared with what it cost

Return on Investment (ROI) The profit your marketing returns compared with what it cost Return on Investment (ROI): How much profit an investment returns compared with what it cost. ROI is the clearest way to judge whether marketing is paying for itself.

What Is Return on Investment? Return on investment, or ROI, measures the profit an investment produces compared with its cost. The formula is (gain from the investment minus cost) divided by cost, times 100. If marketing costing $5,000 produces $15,000 in profit, ROI is 200 percent. Marketing ROI looks at the full picture: ad spend, agency fees, software, content, and staff time on one side, and the profit from new and returning customers on the other.
Why Return on Investment Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses

Why Return on Investment Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses ROI answers the question every owner asks: is marketing paying for itself? A Goshen accounting firm that knows its SEO investment returns several times its cost can invest with confidence instead of treating marketing as an expense to cut. ROI also helps compare very different investments, such as SEO, paid ads, email marketing, and a new website, on equal terms, guiding budget decisions for Northern Indiana businesses. Knowing your ROI also changes conversations with partners, lenders, and staff. Instead of debating whether marketing "works," you can point to clear numbers showing what each channel returned and plan next year's growth with confidence.

How Return on Investment Works Total the costs Include ad spend, fees, tools, and time. Measure the gain Use profit, not just revenue, from customers the marketing produced. Calculate Gain minus cost, divided by cost, times 100. Consider timing Some channels, such as SEO, build returns over months and years. Compare channels Look at ROI by channel to guide future investment.

A Local Example A Warsaw HVAC company invests $18,000 in a year of SEO, Google Ads, and email marketing. Its CRM shows those channels produced customers generating $95,000 in revenue at a 40 percent gross margin, or $38,000 in gross profit. ROI is ($38,000 minus $18,000) divided by $18,000, or about 111 percent. Breaking ROI down by channel reveals email marketing to past customers delivers the highest return, so the company expands its maintenance reminder program.
Getting Started With Return on Investment

Getting Started With Return on Investment Track lead sources for every new customer in a CRM or simple spreadsheet. Without knowing where customers come from, ROI becomes guesswork. Add up all marketing costs for a period, then total the profit from customers those efforts produced. Calculate ROI overall and by channel. Remember that SEO and content often keep producing customers long after the work is done, so review ROI over a full year as well as month to month.
Quick Wins to Improve Your Marketing ROI

Quick Wins to Improve Your Marketing ROI Record the lead source for every new customer Use profit, not revenue, in ROI calculations Include all costs for an honest picture Review ROI by channel every quarter Factor in repeat business and customer lifetime value

What to Watch For Revenue as profit. ROI based on revenue overstates returns. Short time frames. Long-term channels may look weaker in early months. Untracked sources. Referrals and word of mouth often start with marketing. Attribution. Customers often interact with several channels before buying.

Return on Investment FAQ What is a good marketing ROI? Any positive ROI means marketing returns more than it costs. Many businesses aim for several dollars of profit for every dollar spent. How is ROI different from ROAS? ROI measures profit against total cost. ROAS measures revenue against ad spend only. How do I measure ROI for SEO? Track organic leads and customers over time, and compare their profit with the cost of SEO. Should ROI include customer lifetime value? Including lifetime value gives a fuller picture of long-term returns. What costs should be included in marketing ROI? Ad spend, agency or freelancer fees, software subscriptions, content production, and the share of staff time spent on marketing all belong in the calculation. How often should I measure ROI? Quarterly reviews work well, with an annual review for long-term channels. Put It to Work Want clear proof that your marketing pays for itself? t: What Is Review Velocity? Why Steady Reviews Win Local Search
d: Review velocity is the pace at which your business earns new reviews. Learn why steady, recent reviews matter for local rankings and customer trust.
s: Review Velocity The steady pace of new reviews your business earns

Review Velocity The steady pace of new reviews your business earns Review Velocity: How many new reviews your business earns in a set period. A steady flow shows customers and search engines that you are active and trusted.

What Is Review Velocity? Review velocity is the rate at which a business earns new online reviews over time, such as six new Google reviews a month. It looks at the flow of reviews, not just the total count or average rating. Steady velocity shows that real customers keep choosing and talking about your business. A company with 200 reviews but none in the past year looks less active than a competitor with 80 reviews and several new ones every week.
Why Review Velocity Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses

Why Review Velocity Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses Customers notice dates. A Warsaw homeowner comparing contractors trusts recent reviews more than ones from several years ago, because they describe the business as it operates today. Reviews are also a key part of local search prominence, and recency and steady activity help Google and AI tools see your business as established and trusted across Northern Indiana and Michiana.

How Review Velocity Works Total review count The number of reviews you have accumulated. Recency How recently customers left reviews. Steady flow A consistent pace over months, rather than one large burst. Rating and content The average rating and the details customers mention, such as services and towns. Owner responses Thoughtful replies show the business listens.

A Local Example A Goshen auto repair shop has 140 Google reviews, but the newest is ten months old. It starts sending a short text after every completed repair with a direct link to its review form. Within a few months it earns several new reviews each week, many mentioning specific services such as brake repair and alignments. The shop begins appearing more often in the map pack for repair searches around Goshen and Elkhart. Replying to each review also gives the owner a chance to thank customers by name and invite them back for seasonal maintenance.

Getting Started With Review Velocity Choose the moment when customers are happiest, usually right after a job is completed or a purchase is picked up. That is when a review request feels natural and gets the best response. Create a short review link from your Google Business Profile, and send it by text or email with a friendly note. Train your team to mention reviews in person, add the link to receipts and follow-up emails, and reply to every review within a few days. Track new reviews each month to keep the pace steady.
Quick Wins to Improve Your Review Velocity

Quick Wins to Improve Your Review Velocity Send a review link after every completed job or sale Use text messages for faster, higher response Reply to every review within a few days Ask in person at the moment of delight Track new reviews per month as a key metric

What to Watch For Incentives. Google prohibits offering rewards in exchange for reviews. Review gating. Ask every customer the same way, rather than only happy ones. Bursts. A sudden spike of reviews followed by silence looks less natural than steady growth. Fake reviews. Never post or buy reviews; they violate policies and can lead to penalties.

Review Velocity FAQ How many reviews should I get per month? Aim for a steady pace that matches or exceeds top local competitors in your category. Do review replies help rankings? Replies show engagement and build customer trust, and Google encourages businesses to respond. Can I ask customers for reviews? Yes. Google allows businesses to ask for reviews, as long as there are no incentives and every customer is asked fairly. What should I do about a negative review? Reply calmly and professionally, offer to resolve the issue offline, and focus on earning more positive reviews. Do reviews on other sites matter? Yes. Facebook, Yelp, and industry sites add to your reputation, though Google reviews usually matter most for local search. Put It to Work Want a steady stream of fresh reviews? t: What Is an AI Citation? Getting Recommended by AI Tools
d: An AI citation is when ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, or Google AI Overviews references your business or website. Learn how local businesses earn AI citations.
s: AI Citation When AI tools name, quote, or link to your business

AI Citation When AI tools name, quote, or link to your business AI Citation: When an AI tool such as ChatGPT, Gemini, or Perplexity names your website or business as a source in its answer. AI citations send informed, ready-to-act visitors and build your reputation.

What Is AI Citation? An AI citation happens when an AI tool such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot, or Google AI Overviews mentions your business, quotes your content, or links to your website as a source in its answer. Citations can be explicit links to your pages or mentions of your business name in recommendations. They are the AI-era version of ranking well: the sources an AI chooses to trust and share.
Why AI Citation Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses

Why AI Citation Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses More customers now ask AI tools for recommendations, such as "Who is a good roofer in Elkhart?" or "What should I look for in a Goshen daycare?" The businesses named in those answers gain trust instantly, often before the customer visits any website. AI citations also strengthen traditional search. The same signals that earn citations, such as clear content, consistent business information, and strong reputation, also support rankings across Northern Indiana and Michiana.

How AI Citation Works Retrieval AI tools search the web or their index for relevant, trustworthy sources. Selection They favor clear, specific, well-structured content from credible sources. Cross-checking Consistent facts across your website, profiles, and directories increase confidence. Generation The AI writes an answer and may cite the sources it used. Reputation Reviews, mentions, and links help AI recognize your business as established.

A Local Example A Granger orthodontist publishes clear pages answering questions parents ask, such as when children should first see an orthodontist and what treatment costs in the area. It adds FAQ schema, author credentials, and consistent business details across its Google Business Profile and directories. When parents ask AI tools about orthodontists near Granger, the practice is named and its pages are linked as sources. The practice tracks results by asking new patients how they found the office, and a growing number mention AI tools by name.

Getting Started With AI Citation Ask several AI tools the questions your customers ask, such as "best [service] in [your town]" and common how-to or cost questions. Note which businesses and websites they mention and what information they share about you. Then strengthen your sources. Make sure your website clearly states your services, locations, and credentials, answer common questions directly, add schema markup, keep your Google Business Profile and directories consistent, and earn reviews and local mentions. Recheck the same questions every month to track progress.
Quick Wins to Improve Your AI Citations

Quick Wins to Improve Your AI Citations Answer customer questions directly at the top of page sections Keep business details identical across the web Add LocalBusiness and FAQPage schema Show author names, credentials, and real local experience Earn mentions in local news, associations, and directories

What to Watch For Inaccurate answers. Correct wrong facts at the source, such as your website and profiles. Changing tools. AI products update often, so track results across several tools. Crawler access. Allow AI crawlers in robots.txt if you want to be cited. Measuring impact. Ask new customers how they found you to capture AI referrals.

AI Citation FAQ How do AI tools choose which businesses to cite? They favor sources that clearly answer the question, appear trustworthy, and match information found across the web. Can I pay to be cited by AI? Organic AI citations cannot be bought. They are earned through clear content and strong reputation. Is AI citation the same as SEO? They overlap heavily. Answer Engine Optimization and Generative Engine Optimization focus specifically on earning AI citations. Do reviews affect AI recommendations? Reviews are one of the signals AI tools use to judge reputation. Steady, genuine reviews with thoughtful owner replies make your business a more confident recommendation. How can I track AI citations? Check AI tools regularly with customer questions, review referral traffic in analytics, and ask new customers how they found you. t: What Are Google AI Overviews? How They Pick Sources
d: AI Overviews are AI-written summaries at the top of some Google searches. Learn how they choose sources and how local businesses earn citations inside them.
s: AI Overviews Google's AI-written summaries at the top of search results

AI Overviews Google's AI-written summaries at the top of search results AI Overviews: AI-written summaries that Google displays at the top of some search results. They pull information from several websites and present a quick answer above the regular listings.

What Is AI Overviews? AI Overviews are summaries generated by Google's Gemini models that appear at the top of some search results. They answer the question directly, combining information from several web pages, and they include links to the sources they drew from. They appear most often for informational and comparison questions, such as "how often should a furnace be serviced" or "what is the difference between a crown and a filling," and they increasingly appear for local and commercial searches as well.
Why AI Overviews Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses

Why AI Overviews Matters for Northern Indiana & Michiana Businesses AI Overviews sit above traditional results, so the businesses cited inside them gain visibility even when searchers do not scroll. For a Michigan City HVAC company or a South Bend dental office, being the cited source turns a quick question into brand awareness and trust. Many searches now end on the results page. Earning citations in AI Overviews keeps your business visible as search behavior shifts toward instant answers.

How AI Overviews Works Query understanding Google interprets the question and breaks complex queries into related sub-questions. Source retrieval It pulls relevant, trustworthy pages from its search index. Answer generation Gemini writes a summary grounded in those sources. Citations Linked sources appear beside or within the overview, sending clicks to the pages that informed it.

A Local Example A Granger pediatric dentist publishes a clear page answering "When should my child first see a dentist?" with a direct two-sentence answer, a short explanation, an FAQ section with schema, and an author bio. When local parents search the question, Google's AI Overview cites the page, and the practice's name appears at the top of the results.

Getting Started With AI Overviews Search the questions your customers ask most and note which ones show an AI Overview and which sources it cites. Questions like "how much does a new roof cost in Indiana" or "how often should I pump my septic tank" are strong starting points for service businesses across Michiana. Next, make sure your website answers those questions clearly. Lead each section with a direct answer, follow with helpful detail, and add FAQ sections with schema markup. Show who wrote the content and why they know the topic. Keep your Google Business Profile and website facts consistent, since AI tools cross-check them. Then recheck the same searches every month and track branded searches and impressions in Google Search Console to see how your visibility grows.
Quick Wins to Improve Your AI Overview Visibility

Quick Wins to Improve Your AI Overview Visibility Answer common customer questions directly in the first sentences of a section Use clear headings that match how people phrase questions Add FAQPage and LocalBusiness schema Show author expertise and real local experience Keep facts current and consistent with your Google Business Profile

What to Watch For Rankings still matter. AI Overviews draw largely from pages that already rank well. Clicks change. Track impressions and branded searches, not only clicks, to see the full value. Accuracy. Check how AI describes your business and correct inconsistent facts at the source. Availability varies. AI Overviews appear for some searches and not others, and coverage keeps changing.

AI Overviews FAQ Can I opt into AI Overviews? There is no sign-up. Pages are eligible when they are indexed and can appear as snippets in search. Helpful, well-structured content earns citations. Do AI Overviews reduce website traffic? Studies show fewer clicks on some searches with AI Overviews, which makes earning a citation more valuable, since cited sources still receive visibility and clicks. How is this different from featured snippets? Featured snippets quote one page. AI Overviews write a new summary from several sources and cite them.
